title.narrative: Niger Community Action Project for Climate Resilience

description.narrative: The project development objective (PDO) is to improve the resilience of the populations and of production systems to climate changeand variability in targeted Communes.

The project development objective is to improve the resilience of the populations and of production systems to climate change and variability in targeted Communes. These objectives will be achieved through three separate and complementary components: Mainstreaming climate resilience into development strategies at national and local levels; Integrating climate resilience practices into agro-sylvo-pastoral systems and local populations? social protection measures; and Ensuring coordination of all the activities of the project, including monitoring and evaluation activities, and SPCR overall strategic coordination.

comment.narrative:
<p><strong>Original target 112 percent achieved, and revised target 134 percent achieved. </strong>??????The indicator was defined as the number of community facilities vulnerable to the main effects of climate change to be protected or rehabilitated. The original target was set to between 210 and 250 such facilities. When the AF was approved in May 2019, the target value was reduced to 175 even though a total of 221 facilities had already benefitted from sub-project investments. This hints at a mistake that may haveoccurred. At project end, 235 socio-economic facilities had been protected or rehabilitated with the purpose to improve communities’ absorptive capacity against the adverse impact of climate change. The facilities included health centers, child nutrition centers, maternity hospitals, primary schools, markets, slaughterhouses, vaccination parks, feeder roads, water supply systems, small water infrastructure, food storage facilities, among others. Unskilled workers earned paid labor from undertaking physical work involved in protecting and restoring the facilities. Communities relying on the services provided by the facilities are benefiting from a more climate-resilient infrastructure, thereby reducing the community’s overall vulnerability to climate risks such a variability in rainfall. title.narrative: Forage yield increase in the project's areas of intervention

comment.narrative:
<p><strong>Original target 160 percent achieved, and revised target 107 percent achieved. </strong></p>
<p>The indicator relates to both parts of the PDO. It was originally defined as “Reduced forage deficit in targeted agro-pastoral systems within the area covered by the project” with a target of reducing the forage deficit to 600,000 tonnes a year from a baseline with a yearly deficit of 1,817,046 tonnes. Like PDO Indicator 3, it was reworded twice in two level 2 restructurings due to attribution issues (see para. 18). The first revision in December 2014 changed the indicator to “Increased forage production in targeted agro-pastoral systems within the area covered by the project“. At that point the target was changed from an absolute deficit reduction toa relative increase in forage production of 20 percent. The final wording of the indicator was approved in 2019 as part of the AF and read “Forage yield increase in the project's areas of intervention”. The target value was revised to 30 percent and defined as the average forage yield increase across the Project's areas of intervention during a specific year in comparison to neighboring areas not applying improved SLWM practices and where the producers have not been sensitized to the importance of improving climate resilience in their productive systems. In 2020, sampling of dried biomass among 625 farmers in 41 Project and controlsites showed that average forage yields in Project sites were 32 percent higher than average forage yields in control sites. While the sampling was carefully planned to compare areas of similar edaphic and pluvial characteristics, it should be noted here that theanalysis does not include a yield baseline to ascertain the impact of Project investments. The outcome was achieved by introducing SLWM practices, such as establishing pastoral half-moons, planting fodder crops, and controlling invasive plants, on 46,991 hectaresof silvo-pastoral land (intermediate indicator 7), which contributed to increasing forage yields of biomass for fodder.</p>

<p><strong>Original target 442 percent achieved, and revised target 101 percent achieved. </strong></p>
<p>The original target value was defined as 40 percent of the targeted population; equal to 800,000 people. The target population included local authorities, producer groups, women’s associations, and other groups living in targeted Communes. At project end, the Project had reached more than 3.5 million people through wide dissemination of knowledge products produced (intermediate indicator 3).</p>

title.narrative: Additional silvo pastoral areas with improved SLM

comment.narrative: <p><strong>Original target 470 percent achieved, and revised target 124 percent achieved. </strong>The indicator was defined as theadditional hectares of silvo-pastoral land on which farmers had adopted SLWM practices. The original target value of 10,000 hectares was revised upwards twice; first to 26,800 hectares in December 2014 and later to 38,000 hectares in May 2019. At project end, a total of 46,991 hectares of silvo-pastoral land is benefitting from SLWM practices introduced by farmers supported by the Project. This includes: 13,515 ha of pastoral half-moons, 2,943 ha of dune fixation, 22,063 ha with control of invasive species, 213 ha of reforestation, and 25 ha of areas with irrigated fodder crops.</p>

<p><strong>Original target 274 percent achieved, and revised target 176 percent achieved. </strong></p>

<p>Direct Project beneficiaries were defined based on the target area for investments under Component 2. The 38 targeted Project communes covered 310,000 households with an average of 7 people per household for a population of about 2 million people (equal to 13 percent of the population in Niger). The target value of 180,000 households represented 60 percent of all households in the Project area and consisted of threespecific groups of direct Project beneficiaries: rural producers (124,000 households equal to 69% of target), poor households (36,000 households equal to 20% of target), and paid laborers (20,000 households equal to 11% of target). Se<em>e</em> <strong>Table 8</strong>  for an overview. The target value was revised upwards to 280,000 households in May 2019 as part of the AF. The AF does not explain the increase of 100,000 beneficiaries. However, extrapolating the PAD formula to calculate the number of beneficiaries for the extended implementation period based on the activities planned under the AF shows that the number of beneficiaries would reach 280,000 households <em>(</em><strong>Table 9</strong>). At Project closing, direct Project beneficiaries number 493,236 households. These beneficiary households include: (i) 173,101 households benefitting from agricultural support, (ii) 125,421 households benefitting from pastoral support, (iii) 108,356 households benefitting from forest support, and (iv) 86,358 households benefitting from social protection activities. Comparing the result to both the original and revised targets by beneficiary group shows that the Project delivered for both rural producers and poor households (<strong>Table 10</strong>). A more detailed overview of the goods and services delivered to 2.415 million direct beneficiaries, including 1.155 million women, is included in <strong>Table 11</strong> below.</p>

<p><strong>For female beneficiaries.</strong></p>

<p><strong>Original target 80 percent achieved, and revised target 96percent achieved. </strong></p>

<p>The sub-indicator was defined in proportion to PDO indicator 3. The target value was set to 60 percent, implying that 60 percent of direct Project beneficiaries would be females. In May 2019 when the AF was approved, the targetwas reduced to 50 percent of PDO indicator 1 to reflect actual progress. At Project end, females account for 48 percent of direct Project beneficiaries (<strong>Table 11</strong>).</p>

title.narrative: Crop yield increase in the project's areas of intervention

comment.narrative:
<p><strong>Original target 187 percent achieved, and revised target 117 percent achieved.</strong></p>
<p>The indicator relates toboth parts of the PDO. It was originally defined as “Reduced cereal deficit in targeted agro systems within the area covered by the project” with a target of reducing the cereal deficit to 30,000 tonnes a year from a baseline of 100,000 tonnes yearly deficit. However, the indicator was reworded twice in two level 2 restructurings due to attribution issues (see para. 18). It was first revised in December 2014 as “Increased cereal production in targeted agro-pastoral systems within the area covered by the project“. At that point the target was changed from an absolute deficit reduction to a relative increase in cereal production of 30 percent. The final wording of the indicator was approved in 2019 as part of the AF and read “Crop yield increase in the project's areas of intervention”. The target value was revised to 48 percent and defined as the average crop yield increase in different agro-systems across the Project's areas of intervention during a specific year in comparison to neighboring areasnot applying improved SLWM practices and where the producers have not been sensitized to the importance of improving climate resilience in their productive systems. In 2020, a sampling of 275 Project and control sites showed that average crop yields in Project sites were 56 percent higher than average crop yields in control sites (<strong>Table 3</strong>). While the sampling was carefully planned to compare areas of similar edaphic and pluvial characteristics, it should be noted here that the analysis does not include a yield baseline to ascertain the impact of Project investments. For robustness, the ICR undertook further analysis of the entire dataset of annual crop yield samples from 2014 to 2020. Using the departmental crop yield forecasts for 2014 as a base, there is a 46 percentage points spread between the annual yield change in Project sites in 2020 and the annual yield change in control sites in 2020 (<strong>Figure 2</strong>). This was achieved by providing improved seeds, fertilizers, and technical assistance to farmers on anarea of about 166,100 ha of rain-fed agriculture.</p>

title.narrative: Additional agricultural areas with improved SLM

comment.narrative: <p><strong>Original target 202 percent achieved, and revised target 121 percent achieved. </strong>The indicator was defined as theadditional hectares of agricultural land on which farmers have adopted SLWM practices. The original target value of 3,000 hectares was revised upwards twice; first to 4,000 hectares in December 2014 and later to 5,000 hectares in May 2019. At project end, an additional 6,061 hectares of agricultural land are benefitting from SLWM practices introduced by farmers supported by the Project. This includes: 2,072 ha of lowland bowl crops, such as cassava and sweet potato; 1,204 ha of irrigated crops and development of new irrigated sites; and 2,785 ha of previously uncultivated land recovered by use of agricultural half-moons.</p>

title.narrative: Percentage of producers adopting SLM practices introduced by the project

comment.narrative: <p><strong>Original target 128 percent achieved, and revised target 103 percent achieved. </strong>The indicator was defined as thepercentage of rural producers adopting sustainable land and water management practices introduced by the Project. The target value was originally set at 60 percent but was adjusted upward to 75 percent in the May 2019 AF approval. See Section 1A for an overview of SLWM practices introduced by the Project. At project end, a beneficiary survey with a representative sample of 20 agricultural households in 77 villages in the Project intervention zone was implemented with support from the National Statistical Institute. The survey showed that 77 percent of rural producers benefitting from Project support had adopted at least one of the SLWM techniques introduced. The high attainment rate can be attributed in part to the proper testing and adaptation of SLWM techniques to local conditions, and in part to the combination of SLWM practices with social protection measures, such as seed banks and provision of alternative livelihoods.</p>
